en.title: Public Administration: the whole course
en.short: What public administration covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What public administration is
sections.text:
Public administration is the study and practice of how governments and public bodies organise work, make decisions, spend public money and deliver services. It covers the executive machinery of the state, the civil service, public policy, budgeting, procurement, local government, regulation and accountability. It draws on political science, law, economics, management and quantitative methods.

It is wider than the administration of central government. Local councils, public enterprises, agencies, non-governmental organisations and international bodies all raise public administration questions. The subject differs from business administration because public bodies answer to law, taxpayers and political authority, and because they are expected to create public value, meaning benefits to citizens that markets may not supply, rather than profit.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a BSc in Public Administration over four years full-time, under benchmarks from the National Universities Commission. Polytechnics offer ND and HND programmes under the National Board for Technical Education. Master’s awards include the MPA and MSc, and some students continue to PhD.

In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree is often three years and a taught master’s one year. In the United States, a bachelor’s is commonly four years. Many programmes begin with foundational courses, move to core public administration courses, then add electives, a research methods course and a project or dissertation. Accreditation and admission rules change, so confirm details with your department.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics establish the vocabulary and history. You study the nature, scope and study of public administration; its evolution as a discipline; classical and bureaucratic theories; human relations and behavioural theories; politics, administration and the environment; organisation and management principles; administrative law foundations, meaning the law that governs public bodies; economics for the public sector; and quantitative methods and statistics.

Core topics apply these foundations. They include the public policy process; personnel administration and the civil service; public finance and budgeting; public sector accounting and audit; procurement and contract management; ethics and accountability; decentralisation, local government and intergovernmental relations; development administration, the study of how public bodies manage development programmes; comparative public administration; public enterprises, privatisation and regulation; e-government and digital governance, meaning the use of digital tools to deliver public services; project management, monitoring and evaluation; public sector reform and new public management, which applies private sector style management ideas to public bodies; strategic management; public service delivery and quality; and research methods and project work.

Master’s level deepens theory and research. It usually covers advanced theories of public administration; governance, institutions and public value; advanced public financial management and fiscal governance, meaning the rules and institutions that manage public money; and advanced research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn each theory with three questions: what problem does it explain, what does it recommend, and what criticism does it attract? Connect theory to a real public body you know, such as a local council, ministry or agency. For law and finance topics, use the current official rules and say which country they belong to.

Keep a glossary of terms such as public value, accountability, meaning the duty to answer for decisions, decentralisation, meaning the transfer of powers to lower levels, and new public management. For quantitative topics, practise full calculations and check each step. For policy and administration topics, write short answers that define the concept, give an example and assess it. Read past examination questions to see how your department frames problems.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often memorise definitions without understanding the argument. Another common error is to present one country’s civil service rules, budget cycle or local government system as universal. Public administration is comparative, so name the country and the year.

Other mistakes include:
Confusing politics with administration in a simple way, when the two overlap.
Ignoring law, economics or statistics because they seem difficult.
Using old figures for budgets, salaries or pass marks.
Writing a project without a clear research question.
Treating public and private management as identical.
Failing to cite official sources and academic authors.

keyPoints: Public administration studies how public bodies decide, organise, spend and deliver services.
It draws on political science, law, economics, management and quantitative methods.
Degree length and awards vary by country, so check your institution’s handbook.
Study in order: foundations, core applied topics, then advanced theory and research.
Name the country and year whenever you use a rule, figure or institution.
Learn theory with criticism and examples, and practise calculations and past questions.

en.title: The Nature, Scope and Study of Public Administration
en.short: Defining public administration, its scope, approaches, public-private divide and why we study it.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
Public administration is the activity of carrying out government decisions and managing public resources for the public interest. It includes ministries, departments, agencies, local governments and the people who work in them. As a field of study, it examines this work systematically, so the term names both a practice and an academic subject.

Its core is the executive side of government: implementing laws and policies, delivering services, spending public money and keeping records. It is not all of government; legislatures make laws and courts adjudicate, though administrators support both.

sections.heading: Scope and approaches
sections.text:
The scope covers organisation, personnel, finance, policy implementation and service delivery; later topics treat these separately. Three approaches are common. The managerial approach treats public administration as management: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling. The political approach treats it as part of politics, shaped by power, values and public debate. The legal approach stresses laws, rules, fair procedure and judicial review, where courts check legality.

They overlap. A ministry may plan efficiently (managerial), follow a minister’s priorities (political) and obey procurement law (legal).

sections.heading: Public and private
sections.text:
Public administration differs from private administration in ownership, purpose and accountability. A public body is funded mainly by taxes or public charges and must serve the public interest; a private firm serves owners and seeks profit. Public bodies face open scrutiny, legal constraints and political direction. Private firms also face rules, but usually less disclosure.

A simple case: Ngozi is a records officer in a made-up Ministry of Health in Enugu State, Nigeria. She plans a purchase (managerial), follows the ministry’s priorities (political) and obeys public procurement rules (legal). A private clinic manager buying the same forms answers mainly to owners.

sections.heading: Why study it
sections.text: People study public administration to understand government, improve services and accountability, and prepare for public service careers. It helps citizens judge what governments do. Politics sets direction; administration implements. Management supplies tools, but public administration adds accountability and the authority of the state, the organised political community.

keyPoints: Public administration is both the activity of implementing government decisions and the field that studies it.
Its scope includes executive agencies, service delivery, personnel, finance and policy implementation.
Managerial, political and legal approaches are complementary, not exclusive.
Public administration is close to politics and management but is shaped by public accountability and state authority.
Public bodies differ from private firms in ownership, purpose, funding and openness to scrutiny.
Studying the field helps improve services, strengthen accountability and prepare citizens and officials.

en.title: The Evolution of Public Administration as a Discipline
en.short: How public administration became a field, from Wilson and the politics-administration dichotomy to later phases and criticisms.

sections.heading: Origins of the field
sections.text: Public administration is the study and practice of how governments organise and deliver public services. Practice is ancient, but the field of study is modern. Woodrow Wilson’s essay 'The Study of Administration' (1887), written in the United States, is often treated as its starting point. He argued that administration should be studied scientifically and separated from party politics. Frank Goodnow’s Politics and Administration (1900) gave the separation a clearer name: the politics-administration dichotomy. Politics sets policy; administration carries it out. This idea helped the field claim neutrality and expertise, but it was always an ideal rather than a description.

sections.heading: Main phases
sections.text: Textbooks often divide the discipline into phases. The traditional or classical phase, roughly from the 1880s to the 1940s, stressed formal organisation, hierarchy and efficiency. The behavioural and revised phase from the 1940s questioned that narrow focus and brought in human and group behaviour. From the 1960s, development administration and the New Public Administration pressed for relevance, equity and social change. From the 1980s, New Public Management applied market ideas such as competition and performance targets. From the 1990s, governance approaches studied networks, partnerships and shared authority. Dates vary by author, so treat them as broad labels.

sections.heading: Criticisms and case
sections.text: Critics reshaped the field by attacking the dichotomy. Administrators advise ministers, draft rules and choose how policies are applied, so they make policy in practice. A value-free administration is also hard to defend, because public servants allocate scarce resources and must justify choices. Behavioural critics said the field ignored real human behaviour. Later critics said bureaucracy was slow and inward-looking, while governance scholars said government no longer acts alone. In a made-up case, Amina, a state director in Nigeria, is asked to prepare options for a waste-collection policy. She costs the options and recommends one, then implements the chosen plan. Her work mixes policy advice with administration, showing the dichotomy’s limit.

keyPoints: Public administration has been practised for centuries, but its study as a discipline is modern.
Woodrow Wilson’s 1887 essay is often treated as the field’s starting point in the United States.
Frank Goodnow’s 1900 book gave the politics-administration dichotomy its clearer name.
The dichotomy says politics sets policy while administration carries it out.
Critics argue that administrators make policy, cannot be fully value-neutral, and work in networks rather than alone.
The discipline’s phases, from classical to New Public Management and governance, are broad labels with dates that vary by author.

en.title: Classical and Bureaucratic Theories of Administration
en.short: Scientific management, administrative management and Weberian bureaucracy, with strengths and criticisms.

sections.heading: Scientific management
sections.text:
Scientific management studies work to find the most efficient method. Frederick Winslow Taylor, an American engineer, set out its ideas in The Principles of Scientific Management in 1911. Managers should study each job, standardise tools and methods, select and train workers, and separate planning from doing. The aim is efficiency.

In public organisations it can improve routine work such as records handling or revenue collection. Critics say it treats people like machine parts, ignores motivation and can push speed over quality.

sections.heading: Administrative management
sections.text:
Administrative management examines the whole organisation and the manager’s job. Henri Fayol, a French mining engineer, described five functions: planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling. His principles include division of work, authority with responsibility, unity of command and the scalar chain, a clear line of authority from top to bottom. Unity of command means each worker should receive orders from one supervisor only.

These ideas help public agencies assign duties and avoid conflicting instructions. Applied as fixed laws, they can become rigid and block cooperation.

sections.heading: Weberian bureaucracy
sections.text:
Max Weber, a German sociologist, described bureaucracy as an ideal type, a model for analysis rather than a description of every office. Its features include legal-rational authority, which means power based on law and rules rather than tradition or personal ties, hierarchy, written rules, division of labour, impersonal treatment, appointment by merit and a career. Written rules make decisions predictable and protect citizens from favouritism. Hierarchy fixes responsibility. Impersonality means cases are treated by rule, not by who the person knows.

Weber saw this as efficient and fair, but feared it could trap people in routine.

sections.heading: Strengths and criticisms
sections.text:
These theories give public organisations order, consistency and accountability. In a made-up case, Adaeze seeks a trade permit at a state office in Nigeria. Written rules and hierarchy show which desk handles the file and how to appeal. But rules can cause delay, form filling and buck-passing.

Staff may follow procedure when a citizen needs a quick answer. The theories also say little about motivation, discretion and informal organisation.

keyPoints: Scientific management seeks efficiency through job study, standardisation and training.
Administrative management uses Fayol’s functions and principles to coordinate the whole organisation.
Unity of command means one supervisor gives orders to each worker.
Weberian bureaucracy rests on hierarchy, written rules, division of labour and impersonal legal authority.
These theories bring predictability and fairness but can cause rigidity, delay and excessive form filling.
Classical theories pay little attention to motivation, discretion and informal organisation.

en.title: Human Relations and Behavioural Theories
en.short: Hawthorne studies, motivation theories, informal groups and limits in public organisations.

sections.heading: Hawthorne studies
sections.text: The Hawthorne studies were a series of experiments at the Western Electric Hawthorne Works in Cicero, near Chicago, from 1924 to 1932. Researchers, later led by Elton Mayo, studied lighting, rest pauses and hours. Productivity rose in test groups even when conditions returned to normal. The researchers concluded that social attention, group norms and informal relationships influenced work more than physical conditions alone. Later critics showed the methods were weak and that attention from researchers, now called the Hawthorne effect, may explain some results. The studies still shifted attention from machines and rules to people.

sections.heading: Motivation and groups
sections.text: Behavioural approaches ask what encourages people to work well. Maslow’s hierarchy suggests needs move from physiological and safety needs to social, esteem and self-actualisation needs. Herzberg’s two-factor theory separates hygiene factors, such as pay and working conditions, which only prevent dissatisfaction, from motivators, such as achievement and responsibility, which create satisfaction. McGregor’s Theory X assumes workers dislike work and need control; Theory Y assumes they seek responsibility. The informal organisation is the network of friendships, norms and communication that grows alongside the formal structure. Group norms can support or resist official goals. In a made-up district office, clerks slowed work after a new rule. Interviews showed they felt ignored. A monthly staff meeting let them explain problems, and cooperation improved.

sections.heading: Practice and limits
sections.text: These ideas changed management practice. Managers began to consult staff, train supervisors, improve communication and redesign jobs. Participation and teamwork became common. In public organisations, limits remain. Laws, budgets, political direction and public accountability restrict managerial discretion. Pay is often fixed by central rules, and unions are often strong. Citizens are not just customers, and equity matters. Motivation theories have mixed evidence and may not travel across cultures. Behavioural ideas should therefore complement, not replace, structure and rules.

keyPoints: The Hawthorne studies found that social factors and attention can affect productivity, though their methods were criticised.
The Hawthorne effect is a change caused by being observed or given special attention.
Maslow, Herzberg and McGregor offer different views of motivation, and evidence for each is mixed.
The informal organisation consists of social networks and norms that exist alongside formal rules.
Group norms can help or hinder official goals.
Behavioural ideas improve participation but face legal, political and budgetary limits in public organisations.

en.title: Politics, Administration and the Environment of Public Administration
en.short: Politicians and administrators, the dichotomy debate, and how environment shapes administration.

sections.heading: Politicians and administrators
sections.text: Politicians are elected or appointed office holders who make authoritative decisions, set policy and seek public support. Administrators are appointed officials, often civil servants, who advise, implement decisions and manage public resources. Their relationship is complementary but tense. Politicians need administrative capacity and evidence; administrators need lawful direction and legitimacy. In practice their roles overlap, especially where administrators exercise discretion or help draft policy.

sections.heading: The dichotomy debate
sections.text: The politics-administration dichotomy is the idea that politics should set ends and administration should carry them out neutrally and efficiently. Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow are associated with this separation. Critics argue that it is impossible and undesirable. Administrators use discretion, make value choices and influence policy through advice and implementation. Paul Appleby and Dwight Waldo therefore stressed that administration operates within politics. Neutral competence remains an ideal, but complete separation does not exist.

sections.heading: The ecological approach
sections.text: The ecological approach studies how an administration is shaped by its environment. Fred Riggs is a leading name. The political environment includes the regime, laws, accountability and party competition. The economic environment includes resources, inflation, debt and the informal sector. The social environment includes population diversity, inequality and urban or rural conditions. The cultural environment includes beliefs about authority, trust, time and gift giving. Administrators who ignore these pressures design reforms that fail.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: A made-up case: a state government in Nigeria plans a digital land registry. Politicians promise fast results before an election. Administrators know that procurement, staff training and public trust take time. The budget is squeezed by inflation, and many citizens distrust official records. Elders expect face-to-face consultation. A workable plan therefore combines political commitment, realistic funding, staff capacity and local meetings. Ignoring any side of this environment turns a technical project into a political dispute.

keyPoints: Politicians set direction and seek support; administrators advise, implement and manage resources.
The politics-administration dichotomy separates policy from neutral implementation, but critics say discretion makes full separation impossible.
Administrators inevitably make value choices and influence policy.
The ecological approach, associated with Fred Riggs, studies how environment shapes administrative structures and behaviour.
Political, economic, social and cultural conditions can support or undermine reform.
Reforms work better when they fit the local environment and the capacity of administrators.

en.title: Organisation and Management Principles in Public Administration
en.short: Structure, hierarchy, span of control, line and staff, centralisation, delegation and coordination.

sections.heading: Structure and hierarchy
sections.text: Structure is the formal arrangement of units and authority relationships. Hierarchy ranks levels from top to bottom and sets a chain of command. A ministry may have a top administrator, directors over departments, and units below. Hierarchy clarifies reporting and approval. It can also slow communication and distance top managers from lower staff.

sections.heading: Line, staff and span
sections.text: Line functions carry out the main work, such as service delivery. Staff functions advise and support, such as human resources and finance. Staff officers usually have no direct command over line units, so conflict arises when line managers ignore advice or staff act as if they command. Span of control is the number of subordinates reporting to one manager. A narrow span creates many levels and close supervision but slower decisions. A wide span is flatter and cheaper but can overload the manager.

sections.heading: Centralisation and delegation
sections.text: Centralisation keeps authority at the top. Decentralisation gives more authority to field offices and lower levels. Centralisation can produce consistency and control; decentralisation can improve speed and local fit. Delegation is the transfer of authority and responsibility to a subordinate. The manager remains accountable. Clear limits, written instructions and reporting lines make delegation work. Without them, staff may avoid risk or the manager may take work back.

sections.heading: Coordination and conflict
sections.text: Coordination is the alignment of activities so that units work towards shared goals. It needs plans, meetings and clear responsibility. A case: Amina heads a water ministry department. She delegates rural borehole repairs to Chidi, a zonal officer. She keeps approval of large contracts. Chidi coordinates with local government staff and reports monthly. Conflict appears when central procurement delays Chidi’s repairs, or when finance staff reject his requests without explanation. The principles pull against each other: delegation needs trust, central control needs checks, and coordination costs time.

keyPoints: Structure sets formal units and authority relationships; hierarchy ranks levels and creates a chain of command.
Span of control is the number of subordinates reporting to one manager; narrow spans create tall hierarchies and wide spans create flat ones.
Line functions deliver the main work, while staff functions advise and support without direct command.
Centralisation concentrates authority at the top; decentralisation moves authority to field and lower levels.
Delegation transfers authority and responsibility but the manager remains accountable.
Coordination aligns units, and the principles often conflict, so managers must balance control, speed and local fit.

en.title: Administrative Law Foundations
en.short: Rule of law, legality, delegated legislation, discretion, natural justice and judicial review.

sections.heading: Rule of law and legality
sections.text:
Administrative law controls how public authorities use power. The rule of law means government must act under law, not by arbitrary decree. It implies that powers need a legal source, that officials are answerable to courts, and that people affected by decisions should have remedies. Its content differs by country.

Legality is the core principle: a public body may do only what the law authorises, and must follow the limits and procedures in that law. An act outside those limits is ultra vires, meaning beyond the powers. A minister who spends public funds without legal authority acts unlawfully, even if the aim is good.

sections.heading: Delegated legislation and discretion
sections.text:
Delegated legislation is law made by a person or body, such as a minister or agency, under authority given by a parent Act. It saves time and allows technical detail to be updated. But it must stay within the parent Act; courts may strike down rules that exceed it or breach required procedures. Scrutiny and publication rules differ by country.

Administrative discretion is an official’s freedom to choose between lawful options. Discretion is not licence. It must be exercised in good faith, for the purpose the law intended, on relevant facts, and without bias. A decision made for an improper purpose or ignoring relevant evidence can be reviewed.

sections.heading: Natural justice and judicial review
sections.text:
Natural justice, or procedural fairness, requires a fair hearing before decisions affecting rights. Its two rules are audi alteram partem, hear the other side, and nemo judex in causa sua, no one should judge their own cause.

Judicial review checks whether a decision was lawful, not whether it was wise. Courts examine legality, procedural fairness and rationality, and sometimes proportionality. Remedies include quashing the decision. Suppose a licensing officer refuses Amina a permit without hearing her. A court may quash the refusal and order a fresh hearing.

keyPoints: The rule of law requires public authorities to act under law and to be answerable to courts.
Legality means a public body must have legal authority and stay within it; otherwise its act is ultra vires.
Delegated legislation is made under a parent Act and is invalid if it exceeds that Act or breaches required procedures.
Administrative discretion must be exercised in good faith, for a proper purpose, on relevant facts and without bias.
Natural justice requires a fair hearing and an unbiased decision maker.
Judicial review checks the legality, fairness and rationality of administrative action, and its detailed grounds and remedies vary by country.

en.title: Economics for the Public Sector
en.short: Market failure, public goods, externalities, monopoly, equity and the public sector’s roles.

sections.heading: Market failure
sections.text: Market failure means the market, left alone, does not allocate resources efficiently. Examples include public goods, externalities, monopoly and poor information. Efficiency here means society gets the most value from scarce resources. Market failure is not the same as poverty or unfairness; those are equity concerns. Public administration studies how government may correct failure through law, spending, taxes, regulation or direct provision.

sections.heading: Public goods and externalities
sections.text:
A public good is non-rival, so one person’s use does not reduce another’s, and non-excludable, so non-payers cannot easily be kept out. National defence and street lighting are common examples. Because users can free-ride, private firms supply too little, so government may fund or provide the good.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on third parties. In a made-up case, a factory in Kaduna, Nigeria, owned by Adaeze pours waste into a river used downstream. The pollution is a negative externality. Government can tax the polluter, subsidise a beneficial activity such as vaccination, or regulate.

sections.heading: Monopoly and equity
sections.text: A monopoly is a market with a single seller and no close substitutes. Markets with a few large sellers, called oligopolies, raise similar concerns. A monopolist can restrict output and charge higher prices than a competitive market. Government may use competition law, price regulation, or public ownership. Equity arguments are different: even an efficient market may produce incomes or access to services that society judges unfair. Redistribution through taxes and transfers, or ensuring basic services, is then a political choice, not only an economic one.

sections.heading: Public sector roles
sections.text: Public finance textbooks often describe three roles. Allocation means correcting market failure and providing public goods. Distribution means adjusting incomes and access to services. Stabilisation means managing total demand to limit inflation and unemployment, mainly through fiscal and monetary policy. In practice the roles overlap, and choices depend on a country’s laws, budget and politics.

keyPoints: Market failure occurs when markets alone allocate resources inefficiently.
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so free-riding leads to underprovision.
Externalities are third-party costs or benefits that government can tax, subsidise or regulate.
Monopoly power can justify competition law, price regulation or public ownership.
Equity arguments concern fairness of market outcomes, not only efficiency.
The public sector’s roles are allocation, distribution and stabilisation.

en.title: Quantitative Methods and Statistics for Public Administration
en.short: Averages, tables, charts, percentages, probability, sampling and basic inference for administrative data.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a set of observations. The mean is the sum divided by the count. The median is the middle value when the data are ordered, and the mode is the most frequent value. The mean uses every value but is pulled by outliers (extreme values); the median resists them. Spread matters too: range is largest minus smallest, and standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean. In administrative data, report the count and the measure you use, because a mean alone can mislead.

sections.heading: Tables and percentages
sections.text: Put counts in a table with clear row and column labels. A percentage is part ÷ whole × 100. If 240 of 600 surveyed households report a water problem, the percentage is 240 ÷ 600 × 100 = 40%. A bar chart compares categories, a histogram shows the shape of numerical data, and a line chart shows change over time. Always state the base: 40% of 600 is not the same as 40% of 60.

sections.heading: Probability and sampling
sections.text: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 for how likely an event is. For equally likely outcomes, probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. A sample is a smaller group chosen from a population. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection and reduces bias. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. Larger samples usually give more precise estimates, but a biased frame cannot be fixed by size.

sections.heading: Basic inference
sections.text: Inference uses sample results to say something about a population. A sample mean estimates the population mean, but it varies between samples. The standard error measures that variation; for a simple random sample it is s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size. A 95% confidence interval is roughly estimate ± 1.96 × standard error. If a survey finds 40% with a margin of error of 3 points, the plausible range is about 37% to 43%.

keyPoints: Mean = sum ÷ count; the median is the middle ordered value; the mode is the most frequent value.
Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100, and always state the base.
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes for equally likely outcomes.
Random sampling gives every population member a known chance of selection.
The standard error of a sample mean is s ÷ √n for a simple random sample.
A 95% confidence interval is roughly estimate ± 1.96 × standard error.

en.title: The Public Policy Process
en.short: Agenda setting, formulation, decision, implementation and evaluation, with models and gaps.

sections.heading: Stages and actors
sections.text:
Public policy is a course of action or inaction that government chooses to address a public problem. The stages model separates the process into agenda setting, formulation, decision-making, implementation and evaluation. Agenda setting is the struggle to make an issue receive serious government attention. Formulation designs possible responses through officials, experts and stakeholders. Decision-making is the authorised choice made by a cabinet, legislature, minister or court. Implementation turns the choice into rules, spending and services. Evaluation compares outputs and outcomes with aims.

Actors include politicians, civil servants, courts, interest groups, media, citizens and international bodies. Institutions such as the constitution, legislature, bureaucracy and federal arrangements shape who can enter the process and who has authority. The stages are a guide, not a strict sequence.

sections.heading: Models of policy-making
sections.text: The rational-comprehensive model asks decision-makers to clarify goals, compare all options and choose the best. It is an ideal, limited by time, information and politics. Incrementalism, associated with Charles Lindblom, sees policy as small adjustments to existing practice. Mixed scanning, from Amitai Etzioni, combines a broad review with detailed steps. The multiple streams model, from John Kingdon, says problems, policy ideas and politics join at a policy window. The stages model is criticised for seeming too linear.

sections.heading: Gaps and a case
sections.text:
An implementation gap is the difference between what a policy promises and what happens. Causes include vague goals, weak administrative capacity, late or insufficient funds, poor coordination, resistance and political change. Top-down views stress control; bottom-up views stress local context. Street-level bureaucrats, such as teachers and nurses, use discretion when applying rules. Principal-agent problems arise when agencies pursue their own interests rather than the goals of ministers or citizens.

Made-up case: Commissioner Amina’s Nigerian state plans free school meals. Media reports push the issue onto the agenda. Cabinet decides after officials formulate options. Delivery depends on cooks, schools, funds and monitoring. Evaluation asks whether attendance and nutrition improved. If money arrives late or schools lack storage, the gap grows.

keyPoints: Public policy is a course of action or inaction chosen by government to address a public problem.
The stages model covers agenda setting, formulation, decision-making, implementation and evaluation, but is not strictly linear.
Actors and institutions shape which issues reach the agenda and who has authority to decide.
Rational-comprehensive, incremental, mixed scanning and multiple streams models explain different parts of policy-making.
Implementation gaps arise from unclear goals, weak capacity, poor funding, coordination problems and frontline discretion.
Evaluation provides feedback, but policy often changes through politics as well as evidence.

en.title: Public Personnel Administration and the Civil Service
en.short: Civil service structure, recruitment, promotion, training, discipline, pay, appraisal, merit, representation and neutrality.

sections.heading: What the civil service is
sections.text: Public personnel administration manages people employed by government. The civil service is the permanent staff of ministries and agencies. Civil servants are appointed, not elected, and continue when governments change. Structure varies: a country may have a central civil service commission, ministry personnel units and separate local government services. In Nigeria, federal and state civil service commissions handle appointments and promotions. Rules differ by country, so check current regulations.

sections.heading: Recruitment, promotion, training
sections.text: Recruitment should be open and competitive. Posts are advertised, applicants must meet published criteria, and selection may use tests and interviews. Promotion moves an officer to a higher grade. It may rest on merit, seniority, examinations or a mix. Training includes induction and in-service courses. Example: a ministry advertises a supervisor post. Amina scores 80 in appraisal and 70 in interview; Otieno scores 70 and 90. With weights of 60% appraisal and 40% interview, Amina gets 0.6×80 + 0.4×70 = 76, and Otieno gets 0.6×70 + 0.4×90 = 78. Otieno ranks first. If rules also seek regional balance, the commission must state openly how it applies that goal.

sections.heading: Discipline, pay, performance
sections.text: Discipline protects standards. A code of conduct sets expected behaviour, and misconduct may lead to warning, suspension or dismissal after due process. Pay is set in salary scales with allowances and pensions; review bodies or collective bargaining may adjust it. Performance management sets targets, appraises staff and links results to training or promotion. Performance-related pay can weaken teamwork.

sections.heading: Merit, representation, neutrality
sections.text: Merit means choosing and rewarding people for ability and performance. Representation means the service should reflect the public it serves, including regions, gender and ethnic groups. Political neutrality means civil servants serve whichever party is in power, give advice honestly and do not campaign for a party. These values can conflict. A merit-only rule may leave some groups underrepresented; a quota may seem unfair. Countries resolve the tension differently through laws and published rules. The aim is a competent service that the public trusts.

keyPoints: Public personnel administration covers recruitment, promotion, training, discipline, pay and appraisal of government staff.
The civil service is permanent and appointed, not elected.
Merit, representation and political neutrality are central values that can conflict.
Recruitment and promotion should follow published, competitive rules.
Performance management links targets and appraisal to training or promotion.
Rules on civil service structure and pay differ by country, so check current regulations.

en.title: Public Finance and Budgeting
en.short: Government revenue, expenditure, the budget cycle, formats and control, with fiscal discipline and transparency.

sections.heading: Revenue and expenditure
sections.text: Public finance is the study of how government raises, allocates and controls money. Revenue comes mainly from taxes, fees and charges, fines, grants and royalties from natural resources. Borrowing is not income; it is financing that must be repaid with interest. Expenditure is usually split into recurrent spending, such as salaries, drugs and interest, and capital spending, such as roads and schools. The legal rules for each country differ, so check the constitution and finance law.

sections.heading: The budget cycle
sections.text: The budget is the government’s annual financial plan and legal authority to spend. The budget cycle has four main stages: preparation by the executive, approval by the legislature, execution by ministries and agencies, and audit and evaluation after the year ends. Many countries use a medium-term expenditure framework (MTEF), which sets spending ceilings for several years. Fiscal years and legal deadlines vary by country.

sections.heading: Types and formats
sections.text: Budget types include operating (current) and capital budgets, and balanced, surplus or deficit budgets. Formats shape behaviour. A line-item format lists inputs such as salaries and fuel. A programme format groups spending by policy objective. A performance or output-based format links money to measurable results. Zero-based budgeting rebuilds each item from zero, while incremental budgeting starts from last year’s figure. Programme and performance formats make the budget-policy link clearer.

sections.heading: Control and discipline
sections.text: Budgetary control compares plans with actual spending. Techniques include cash limits, commitment control (recording orders before payment), rules on virement (moving funds between items), variance analysis, internal audit, legislative oversight and performance monitoring. Example: a ministry is allocated 12,000,000 for drugs and spends 13,500,000. Variance = 13,500,000 − 12,000,000 = 1,500,000 overspend. Overspend rate = 1,500,000 ÷ 12,000,000 = 0.125, or 12.5%. Fiscal discipline means keeping spending within approved revenue and borrowing plans. Transparency means published, clear and timely budget reports, independent audit and public access. A budget links policy to action: a policy without costing and funding remains an aspiration.

keyPoints: Public finance covers government revenue, expenditure and financial control.
The budget cycle runs from preparation and legislative approval to execution, audit and evaluation.
Recurrent spending covers day-to-day costs; capital spending creates assets.
Line-item, programme and performance formats present budgets differently and shape decisions.
Variance = actual spending − budgeted spending; overspend rate = variance ÷ budget.
Fiscal discipline and transparency require clear rules, timely reports, independent audit and public access.

en.title: Public Sector Accounting and Audit
en.short: Public sector reporting, fund accounting, internal and external audit, and audit institutions.

sections.heading: Reporting and funds
sections.text:
Public sector financial reporting shows how public money was raised, spent and held. A public body often aims at service, not profit. Many governments use accrual accounting, which records income when earned and expenses when incurred, or cash accounting, which records cash received and paid. The International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS), issued by the International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (IPSASB), are used or adapted in many countries. Others follow national rules, such as the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) for state and local governments in the United States, so standards differ.

Fund accounting keeps resources for separate purposes in distinct, self-balancing sets of accounts. A grant for rural water supply is recorded in its own fund and cannot be spent on salaries. This protects restrictions and makes compliance easier to check.

sections.heading: Internal and external audit
sections.text: Internal audit is an independent appraisal inside the organisation. It checks controls, risk and value for money, meaning economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and reports to management or audit committee. External audit is done by an independent auditor outside the body. It gives an opinion on whether the financial statements are fairly presented and may report on compliance and performance. The auditor reports to the legislature or the public, not to managers being audited. Independence and competence are essential.

sections.heading: Audit institutions and case
sections.text:
Supreme audit institutions (SAIs) are the public bodies that audit government accounts. Examples include an Office of the Auditor-General. Many follow the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAIs) from INTOSAI, the international organisation of SAIs, but mandates and standards vary by country. Some audit all public bodies; others central government only.

Case: a state water agency receives a grant for boreholes. Fund accounting keeps the grant separate. Internal audit finds that a contract was split to avoid tender rules. External audit reports the weakness to the state legislature. The legislature questions the agency and orders recovery. This is the accountability chain: managers answer to the public through the legislature and the auditor.

keyPoints: Public sector reporting may use cash or accrual accounting, and standards differ by country.
Fund accounting separates resources that are restricted to particular purposes.
Internal audit is an independent check inside the organisation; external audit is an independent check from outside.
External auditors report to the legislature or the public, supporting accountability.
Supreme audit institutions audit public accounts, but their powers and standards vary by country.
IPSAS and INTOSAI ISSAIs are international reference points, not universal law.

en.title: Public Procurement and Contract Management
en.short: Procurement principles, tendering, bid evaluation, contract award and managing public contracts.

sections.heading: Principles and value
sections.text: Public procurement is how public bodies buy goods, works (construction) and services. Its principles are transparency, open competition, fairness, accountability and value for money. Value for money means the best use of public funds over the whole life of the purchase, not simply the lowest price. A cheap vehicle that is costly to maintain may be poor value. Procurement rules and thresholds differ by country; check the current law and guidance. Nigeria’s Public Procurement Act 2007 established the Bureau of Public Procurement.

sections.heading: Methods and tendering
sections.text: Common methods include open tendering, restricted tendering, requests for quotations and direct procurement. Open tendering invites any qualified supplier to bid and is preferred for large or risky purchases. Direct procurement, also called single-source, is reserved for narrow cases such as urgency or a sole supplier. Tendering steps include advertising, issuing bidding documents, receiving sealed bids, public opening and evaluation. Specifications must be clear and neutral so that they do not favour one bidder.

sections.heading: Evaluation and award
sections.text: Evaluation first checks eligibility and responsiveness (meeting stated requirements), then scores technical quality and price using weights stated in the bidding documents. Suppose price carries 60 points and quality 40. Bid A costs ₦6 million and scores 30 for quality; Bid B costs ₦8 million and scores 38. Price score = lowest price ÷ bid price × 60. A gets 60, B gets 45. Totals: A 90, B 83. Award goes to A if responsive and the rules require the highest total. The award must be published with reasons and a complaints route.

sections.heading: Contract management and risks
sections.text: Contract management runs from signature to completion: mobilisation, milestones, payment against verified delivery, controlled variations (changes), records, disputes and final acceptance. Weak contract management invites corruption. Risks include collusion, bid rigging, conflict of interest, bribery, inflated prices, phantom contracts and unjustified change orders. Controls include separation of duties, published awards, audit trails, independent inspection and payment only after evidence. Transparency and competition reduce risk, but they do not replace active monitoring.

keyPoints: Public procurement uses public funds to buy goods, works and services under transparency, competition, fairness, accountability and value for money.
Value for money considers whole-life cost and quality, not just the lowest bid.
Open tendering is preferred for large purchases, while direct procurement is exceptional and must be justified.
Evaluation must use criteria and weights stated in the bidding documents before bids are opened.
Price score = lowest responsive price ÷ bid price × available price points.
Contract management links payment to verified delivery and controls variations, records and disputes.

en.title: Administrative Ethics and Accountability
en.short: Ethical standards, codes, conflict of interest, whistleblowing, accountability bodies and corruption.

sections.heading: Ethical standards and codes
sections.text:
Administrative ethics are the standards of right conduct expected of public officials: honesty, impartiality, fairness, confidentiality and stewardship of public resources. A code of conduct turns these values into rules, such as limits on gifts, asset declarations and duties to avoid private work that clashes with public office. Codes work only when enforced by training, advice and sanctions.

A conflict of interest arises when a public officer’s private interest could improperly influence official duty. The usual response is to declare the interest and withdraw from the decision. This protects both the decision and the officer’s reputation.

sections.heading: Whistleblowing and accountability
sections.text:
Whistleblowing is the disclosure by an insider of wrongdoing in an organisation. It can expose fraud, unsafe practice or abuse of power. Protection varies by country: the United States has the Whistleblower Protection Act 1989, and the United Kingdom has the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998. Where legal protection is weak, fear of retaliation discourages reports.

Accountability means answerability for decisions and consequences. Mechanisms include legislatures, which question ministers and use public accounts committees; courts, which review legality through judicial review; ombudsmen, who investigate maladministration; auditors; and internal discipline. South Africa’s Public Protector and Nigeria’s Public Complaints Commission are ombudsman-type bodies. These mechanisms work best together.

sections.heading: Corruption and integrity
sections.text:
Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. It includes bribery, nepotism, procurement fraud and extortion. Integrity systems combine clear codes, transparent decisions, asset declarations, audits, complaint channels and enforcement. Nigeria’s Code of Conduct Bureau receives asset declarations from public officers, and its anti-corruption commissions investigate offences. Such bodies need independence and resources.

A made-up case: Ngozi, a procurement officer, is evaluating a bid from her cousin’s firm. She declares the relationship, withdraws from the evaluation, and the committee records the decision. The bid is judged on published criteria. The case shows that ethics is not only a code on paper; it is a habit of disclosure and a system that supports it.

keyPoints: Ethics sets standards of conduct, and a code of conduct turns values into enforceable rules.
A public officer should declare a conflict of interest and withdraw from the decision.
Whistleblowing exposes wrongdoing, but legal protection for whistleblowers differs by country.
Accountability means answerability, supported by legislatures, courts, ombudsmen and auditors.
Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain, so integrity needs transparency and enforcement.
Country examples include South Africa’s Public Protector and Nigeria’s Code of Conduct Bureau.

en.title: Decentralisation, Local Government and Intergovernmental Relations
en.short: Devolution, deconcentration, delegation, local government finance and intergovernmental relations.

sections.heading: Three forms
sections.text: Decentralisation means moving authority and responsibility away from central government. It takes three main forms. Deconcentration spreads central administrative tasks to field offices, but those offices remain under central control. Delegation gives specific powers to semi-autonomous bodies or local officials, while the centre keeps ultimate authority. Devolution transfers powers and resources to elected local governments with their own legal status. Devolution is the strongest form because local councils can decide and be held accountable locally. Countries mix the forms, and the labels are used loosely in practice.

sections.heading: Structure and finance
sections.text: Local government is the lowest tier of public authority below central or regional government. Its structure varies. Unitary countries usually create local councils by national law. Federal countries, such as Nigeria, may give local government constitutional recognition, but state or provincial governments often supervise it. Councils may be one-tier or two-tier, urban or rural. Finance comes from three main sources: own revenue such as property rates, fees and licences; intergovernmental transfers, including shared taxes and grants; and borrowing, usually limited by law. Own revenue gives discretion. Transfers reduce horizontal imbalances (gaps between areas) but can carry conditions. Fiscal decentralisation is the share of public money raised and spent locally.

sections.heading: Autonomy and delivery
sections.text: Intergovernmental relations are the formal and informal links between central, regional and local bodies. Local autonomy means real discretion over budgets, staff and decisions. It is often limited by central rules, unfunded mandates (duties without money) and weak own revenue. Service delivery depends on money, staff skills and accountability. In a made-up case, a district assembly in Ghana funds a market: 40% from market fees and 60% from a central grant. The grant requires reports, and a ministry approves the design. The assembly chooses the site, so it has partial autonomy; the conditions limit its discretion. Systems differ by country, so check the law and current finance rules.

keyPoints: Decentralisation transfers authority from central government; devolution is the strongest form.
Deconcentration keeps field offices under central control; delegation gives limited powers while the centre retains ultimate authority.
Local government finance usually combines own revenue, intergovernmental transfers and limited borrowing.
Local autonomy means real discretion, but rules, unfunded mandates and weak revenue often limit it.
Intergovernmental relations cover formal and informal links between central, regional and local bodies.
Systems differ by country, so check the relevant constitution, statutes and current grant rules.

en.title: Development Administration: State, Capacity and the Developmental State
en.short: State roles, capacity building, planning, poverty reduction, aid, public-private coordination and developmental state debates.

sections.heading: The state as developer
sections.text: Development administration is the part of public administration that guides social and economic change. The state sets direction, supplies public goods such as roads and health care, and corrects market failures. Public administrators turn plans into budgets, projects and services. This role is contested: some argue the state should lead, while others stress markets and private initiative. Most countries mix both.

sections.heading: Capacity, planning and poverty
sections.text:
Capacity building means strengthening the skills, systems and institutions a state needs to plan and deliver. Without it, plans remain paper. Development planning sets medium- and long-term goals and allocates resources. Poverty reduction uses tools such as cash transfers, public works and free basic services, often targeted at poor households. Targeting needs reliable data, or benefits leak.

Consider a made-up case. A district in Ghana wants to reduce child malnutrition. It combines health, agriculture and water plans, trains clinic staff, and contracts local food suppliers. A donor offers money but demands its own reporting. The district negotiates to use its own budget system with joint audits. This builds capacity and keeps ownership.

sections.heading: Aid and coordination
sections.text: Aid is official development assistance: grants and concessional loans from governments and multilateral bodies. It can fund capacity and services, but may create dependency, fragment reporting and bypass local systems. The Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness (2005) set principles: ownership by the recipient, alignment with local systems, harmonisation among donors, managing for results, and mutual accountability. Public-private coordination means government and firms share information, infrastructure and risk. Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are long-term contracts, not free money.

sections.heading: The developmental state debate
sections.text: A developmental state intervenes strategically to promote growth and industrialisation. Chalmers Johnson studied Japan’s Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI). Later writers added South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore. Such states need a capable bureaucracy and 'embedded autonomy': close links with business without capture (Peter Evans). Critics warn of rent-seeking and poor information. Whether the model can be copied in Africa is debated; context and institutions matter.

keyPoints: Development administration is the part of public administration that guides social and economic change.
State capacity, meaning skills, systems and institutions, determines whether plans are implemented.
Poverty reduction needs reliable targeting data and coordinated basic services.
Aid can help but must respect recipient ownership and align with local systems.
A developmental state uses strategic intervention and a capable bureaucracy, but it is not easily copied.
Public-private coordination and PPPs require careful design and risk sharing.

en.title: Comparative Public Administration
en.short: How to compare civil service models, governance traditions, policy transfer and convergence.

sections.heading: Why compare systems
sections.text: Comparative public administration is the systematic study of similarities and differences in public administration across countries. It asks how history, law, politics and culture shape bureaucracy, and it can test theories, inform reform and expose assumptions. An administrative tradition is the inherited set of ideas and practices that shapes how a state organises its public service. A civil service model is the set of rules for recruitment, career, neutrality and accountability. Career-based systems recruit at the bottom, promote internally and value generalist service. Position-based systems advertise specific posts and may bring in outsiders. The Westminster tradition, found in the United Kingdom and many Commonwealth countries including Nigeria and Ghana, stresses a permanent civil service and ministerial responsibility. Many continental European systems give law and legal training a central place.

sections.heading: Transfer and convergence
sections.text: Policy transfer is the process by which ideas, institutions or practices from one jurisdiction are used in another. Lesson drawing is voluntary learning; diffusion spreads through networks and international organisations; coercion occurs when donors or stronger states attach conditions. Convergence means systems becoming more alike, for example through new public management, digital government and international standards. Divergence persists because colonial legacies, legal families, federal arrangements, party politics and state capacity differ. Convergence claims are often overstated: similar labels can hide different practices.

sections.heading: Limits and a case
sections.text: Comparison has limits. Terms such as civil service or accountability may mean different things. Data may be unreliable or collected differently. Ethnocentrism means judging another system by the standards of one’s own. Copying a reform without adapting it to local law, budgets and skills often fails. Consider a made-up case. Aisha, a director in Kano State, Nigeria, studies a performance appraisal system used in Ghana’s civil service. She can copy the form, but Ghana’s personnel records, training and legal rules differ from Kano’s. The form alone will not improve performance; the supporting system must also be adapted.

keyPoints: Comparative public administration studies similarities and differences in administrative systems across countries.
Civil service models differ in recruitment, career paths, neutrality and accountability.
Policy transfer can be voluntary lesson drawing, networked diffusion or coercive conditionality.
Convergence is real but partial; history, law and capacity keep systems different.
Comparison must avoid ethnocentrism and unreliable data.
Reforms copied from abroad usually need adaptation to local institutions.

en.title: Public Enterprises, Privatisation and Regulation
en.short: State ownership, SOE governance and performance, the privatisation debate, and utility regulation.

sections.heading: Why state ownership
sections.text: A state-owned enterprise (SOE) is a company owned or controlled by government. Governments create SOEs to correct market failure, such as natural monopoly in water or electricity networks, where one supplier is cheapest. They pursue strategic goals, public goods, universal service and development where private capital is scarce. Nationalisation is the transfer of private assets into public ownership. Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are long contracts sharing risk between government and private firms, not full privatisation.

sections.heading: Governance and performance
sections.text: SOE governance involves ministers, boards, managers and regulators. A principal-agent problem arises because managers may pursue their own goals rather than the public owner’s. Soft budget constraints mean losses are covered by subsidies or debt relief, weakening efficiency. Performance is mixed. SOEs can provide stable services and protect jobs, but may suffer political interference, weak accounting, overstaffing and corruption. Compare results with targets, audited accounts and sector benchmarks. Outcomes differ by country and sector, so check official reports.

sections.heading: The privatisation debate
sections.text: Privatisation is the sale or transfer of public assets to private owners. Supporters argue it improves efficiency through competition, hard budgets and investment, and reduces fiscal burdens. Critics reply that private owners may cut jobs, raise prices, neglect poorer users or sell strategic assets. Gains depend on market structure and contract design. A made-up case: a state water utility loses money. Selling it without a regulator may let the buyer raise tariffs. Keeping it may preserve subsidies but continue weak service. The choice is not only public versus private.

sections.heading: Regulating utilities
sections.text: After privatisation, natural monopolies need regulation. Economic regulation controls entry, prices, quality and investment, often through an independent regulator using cost and performance data. Price-cap regulation limits tariff rises, with adjustments for inflation and efficiency. Social regulation protects safety, health, environment and consumers, and may impose universal service obligations, meaning service to all at affordable terms. Regulation needs legal independence, transparency, appeal rights and funding. Where tariffs cannot cover costs, government should make subsidies explicit rather than hide them.

keyPoints: State-owned enterprises exist to address market failure, strategic needs and universal service, not only profit.
SOE performance depends on governance, hard budget constraints, competition and clear accountability.
Privatisation can improve efficiency but may harm affordability, employment and strategic control unless contracts and regulation are strong.
Natural monopolies need economic regulation of prices, entry, quality and investment.
Social regulation protects safety, health, environment and consumers, and can include universal service obligations.
Regulation works best with an independent regulator, transparency, appeal rights and explicit subsidies.

en.title: E-Government and Digital Governance
en.short: E-government models, digital services, data systems, inclusion, privacy, security and project risks.

sections.heading: Models and services
sections.text: E-government is the use of information and communication technology (ICT) by public bodies to deliver services and support administration. Digital governance is the wider use of digital tools and data in public decisions and accountability. Common models describe who is served: government to citizen (G2C), government to business (G2B), government to government (G2G) and government to employee (G2E). Maturity models often move from information, to interaction, to transactions such as online payment, and finally to transformation, where processes are redesigned. The stages are a guide, not a law; countries differ.

sections.heading: Data and delivery
sections.text: Digital service delivery means providing public services through websites, mobile apps, portals or shared service centres. It depends on data and information systems: civil registries, land records, payroll systems, management information systems (MIS) and geographic information systems (GIS). Interoperability, the ability of systems to exchange data, lets a citizen update an address once. Open data, published for reuse, can support accountability. But a portal is only the front door; back-office integration and reliable records do the work.

sections.heading: Inclusion, privacy, security
sections.text: Digital inclusion means fair access to digital services regardless of income, location, age, disability, language or skills. Without it, online-only services exclude people. Privacy concerns personal data. Data protection laws differ by country; Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 is one example. Cybersecurity protects confidentiality, integrity and availability of systems. Threats include phishing, ransomware and insider misuse. Agencies need access controls, backups, incident response and staff training.

sections.heading: Project risks and case
sections.text: Technology projects often fail through unclear goals, scope creep (uncontrolled growth of requirements), weak capacity, poor procurement and vendor lock-in, where changing supplier becomes costly. A made-up district council, Mawuli, launches an online permit service. It expects 1,000 permits a year. It receives 600 online applications; 200 fail because applicants lack digital ID or network access, so staff re-enter paper forms. The council adds a help desk and SMS reminders. The lesson: plan for inclusion, training and back-office change, not only the website.

keyPoints: E-government uses ICT to deliver public services and support administration.
The common models are G2C, G2B, G2G and G2E, and maturity stages vary.
Digital service delivery needs interoperable back-office data systems, not just a website.
Digital inclusion requires access, affordability, skills and accessible design.
Privacy and cybersecurity need clear legal rules, access controls, backups and incident response.
Technology projects fail when goals, capacity, procurement and vendor lock-in are ignored.

en.title: Project Management, Monitoring and Evaluation
en.short: Project cycles, logframes, indicators, monitoring and evaluation designs, and how evidence informs policy.

sections.heading: Project cycle and logic
sections.text:
A public project is a time-bound set of activities with a budget and intended results. The project cycle usually runs through identification, design, appraisal, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and closure. Findings can send a programme back to design.

A logical framework, or logframe, is a matrix linking inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact. Inputs are resources such as staff and money. Activities are what the team does. Outputs are direct products, such as training sessions. Outcomes are changes in behaviour or access. Impact is longer-term change. The logframe also states assumptions, indicators and means of verification, the sources used to check each indicator.

sections.heading: Indicators and monitoring
sections.text:
An indicator is a measurable sign of change. A baseline is the value before the project, a target is the expected value by a stated date, and means of verification are where evidence comes from. Good indicators are specific, measurable and tied to the result. Monitoring is routine data collection on activities, outputs and early outcomes. It checks whether implementation is on track and lets managers correct problems.

A case: a health team plans 1,000 antenatal visits in a year, with a mid-year target of 500. By June it records 450 visits. Achievement against the mid-year target is 450 ÷ 500 = 90%. Monitoring shows a gap; the team can ask whether staff, transport or record-keeping caused it.

sections.heading: Evaluation and use
sections.text:
Evaluation is a periodic judgement of a programme’s relevance, design, implementation and results. Formative evaluation happens during implementation and improves the programme. Summative evaluation judges results later. Process evaluation examines delivery; outcome and impact evaluation examine changes. Designs include before-and-after comparison, comparison groups and randomised controlled trials. Random assignment can support causal claims but is not always ethical or practical. Quasi-experimental designs use comparison groups without random assignment.

Evidence feeds policy when findings are timely, clear and discussed with officials. Evaluation supports accountability by reporting against targets and learning by explaining why results happened. It should be independent and transparent.

keyPoints: The project cycle links identification, design, appraisal, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and closure.
A logframe links inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact, with assumptions, indicators and means of verification.
An indicator needs a baseline, target and means of verification.
Monitoring is continuous; evaluation is periodic and judges relevance, implementation and results.
Achievement against target = actual ÷ target × 100%.
Evaluation supports accountability and learning when it is timely, independent and transparent.

en.title: Public Sector Reform and New Public Management
en.short: NPM reforms, market-type mechanisms, performance contracts, decentralisation, new public governance and criticisms.

sections.heading: What NPM changed
sections.text: New Public Management (NPM) is a set of reforms, prominent from the 1980s, that applied private-sector ideas to government. It stressed clear objectives, measurable outputs, competition and managerial autonomy. Instead of rules and inputs, managers were held responsible for results. Agencification separated policy advice from service delivery: the United Kingdom’s Next Steps programme from 1988 turned many civil service units into executive agencies with chief executives and framework documents. NPM spread unevenly; countries adapted it to their own law and capacity.

sections.heading: Market-type mechanisms
sections.text: Market-type mechanisms use competition or prices inside public services. Contracting out means a public body pays an outside provider to deliver a service under a contract. Competitive tendering invites bids. Internal markets make public units buy and sell from one another. User charges make users pay directly for a service, while vouchers give users purchasing power to buy it from approved providers. These tools can improve cost awareness, but they need good contracts, information and monitoring.

sections.heading: Contracts and decentralisation
sections.text: Performance contracts are agreements between a government and an agency or manager. They state outputs, targets, resources and sometimes rewards or penalties. Decentralised management moves authority to agencies and frontline managers, often called 'let managers manage'. The aim is faster decisions and clearer responsibility. Risks include weak central steering, duplicated functions and loss of control.

sections.heading: Later ideas and criticism
sections.text: New public governance sees services as delivered through networks of public, private and community actors. It emphasises trust, collaboration, co-production (users and communities helping to deliver services) and whole-system outcomes rather than single-agency targets. Critics say NPM can fragment services, encourage gaming of indicators (meeting the measure rather than the real goal), impose transaction costs and neglect equity and citizenship. Market reforms may work poorly where competition or contract management capacity is weak. Later reforms therefore combine managerial tools with collaboration, public value and stronger accountability.

keyPoints: NPM applies private-sector ideas such as objectives, outputs and managerial autonomy to public organisations.
Market-type mechanisms include contracting out, competitive tendering, internal markets, user charges and vouchers.
Performance contracts set outputs, targets and accountability between government and agencies or managers.
Decentralised management gives agencies and frontline managers more decision authority.
New public governance stresses networks, trust, collaboration and co-production.
Criticisms include fragmentation, gaming of indicators, transaction costs and neglect of equity.

en.title: Strategic Management in the Public Sector
en.short: Strategic planning, vision, environmental analysis, strategy, targets, stakeholders and public value.

sections.heading: Direction and analysis
sections.text: Strategic management is the continuous work of setting a public organisation’s direction, aligning its resources and adapting to change. Strategic planning is the structured part of that work. It starts with a vision, the desired future, and a mission, the organisation’s purpose and legal mandate. Environmental analysis then scans the setting. PESTLE examines political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental pressures outside. SWOT examines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats inside and outside. In public bodies, laws, budgets and political authorisation limit what is possible.

sections.heading: Formulating strategy
sections.text: Strategy formulation turns analysis into strategic issues and choices. Officials compare options against public value, feasibility, legitimacy and affordability. Public value means outcomes citizens value, such as better health or safer streets, plus trust in public institutions. It is broader than profit or efficiency. Stakeholders include citizens, ministers or councillors, staff, unions, contractors and community groups. Consultation and negotiation build support. Yet accountability for the final choice stays with the legally responsible officials.

sections.heading: Implementation and targets
sections.text: Implementation converts strategy into budgets, structures, duties, timelines and performance targets. A target is a measurable commitment. Targets help monitor progress, but poorly chosen ones can encourage gaming, where staff meet the number while harming the service, or neglect unmeasured work. Balanced measures and regular review reduce this risk. In a made-up case, a district health office in Ghana, led by Director Amina, sets the vision of every child vaccinated on time. Environmental analysis finds staff shortages and weak outreach. The strategy uses mobile clinics with community leaders. The target is to raise monthly reporting from 60% to 85% of clinics within one year. Mothers, staff and the council are consulted, and progress is reviewed quarterly.

keyPoints: Strategic planning sets direction, but implementation depends on budgets, people and political support.
A vision states the desired future, while a mission states purpose and legal mandate.
PESTLE scans the external environment, while SWOT covers internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
Public value includes outcomes citizens value and trust in institutions, not only efficiency.
Performance targets need balanced measures and review to reduce gaming.
Stakeholders shape strategy, but accountability stays with responsible public officials.

en.title: Public Service Delivery and Quality
en.short: Service standards, charters, access, responsiveness, co-production and why delivery fails.

sections.heading: Standards and charters
sections.text: Service standards are explicit commitments about timeliness, accuracy, courtesy and redress. A citizen charter is a public document that states what users can expect and how to complain. The United Kingdom’s Citizen’s Charter, launched in 1991, popularised the idea, but charters now vary widely. A useful charter is specific, measurable and linked to staff duties. Vague promises such as 'prompt service' cannot be monitored or enforced.

sections.heading: Access and responsiveness
sections.text: Access means that services are reachable in practice: physically, financially, digitally, linguistically and for people with disabilities. Responsiveness is the speed and sensitivity with which an office reacts to users’ needs and complaints. Access without responsiveness produces queues and frustration. A clinic may be near a village, yet be unresponsive if staff keep irregular hours. Good managers track waiting times, complaint resolution and opening hours.

sections.heading: Co-production and measurement
sections.text: Co-production treats citizens as partners in designing and delivering services, not passive recipients. Examples include community health volunteers and user panels. Service quality is measured with citizen surveys, administrative data, mystery shopping and complaint analysis. SERVQUAL, developed by Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry, compares expectations with perceptions across reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles. Reliability, meaning doing what was promised, is often rated most important.

sections.heading: Why delivery fails
sections.text: Delivery fails when standards are unclear, funding is short, staff lack skills, coordination is weak, feedback is poor or corruption diverts resources. Unrealistic targets and political interference also distort effort. Suppose a district water office promises repairs within three days but has one vehicle and no spare parts. Waiting times rise, complaints are ignored and trust falls. Failure is rarely one person’s fault; it is a system problem.

keyPoints: Service standards are measurable commitments on timeliness, accuracy, courtesy and redress.
A citizen charter tells users what to expect and how to complain.
Access covers physical, financial, digital, language and disability barriers.
Responsiveness is how quickly and sensitively staff react to needs and complaints.
Co-production makes users partners in service design and delivery.
Service quality is measured by surveys, administrative data, mystery shopping and complaint analysis; delivery failure usually has systemic causes.

en.title: Research Methods and Project Work in Public Administration
en.short: Designing, proposing and carrying out an undergraduate public administration project.

sections.heading: Design and literature
sections.text:
