Research design is the plan for answering your question. A quantitative design uses numbers and often tests hypotheses. A qualitative design explores meanings through words. A mixed design combines both. A cross-sectional design collects data at one time; a case study examines one unit in depth. Choose the design that fits the question.

A literature review groups earlier studies by theme, compares findings and methods, and shows the gap your project addresses. Use peer-reviewed articles, official reports and reliable textbooks, and cite sources.

sections.heading: Sampling and tools
sections.text:
Sampling means selecting part of a population, the whole group your question is about. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. Probability sampling gives every listed unit a known chance of selection, as in simple random sampling. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive sampling, selects units for a reason and cannot support broad generalisation.

Questionnaires suit many respondents and fixed questions. Interviews allow follow-up and depth but take time. Pilot-test both and avoid leading questions.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text:
Data analysis turns raw data into answers. For numbers, use frequencies, percentages and averages; check totals. For interviews, transcribe and group repeated ideas into themes. Do not claim more than the data show.

Research ethics protect people and trust. Seek informed consent, explain the purpose, and make participation voluntary. Keep promises of anonymity, where identity is hidden, and confidentiality, where data are not shared. Protect stored data and avoid harm. Many institutions require ethical approval.

sections.heading: Proposal and findings
sections.text:
A proposal states the title, background, problem, questions, objectives, literature gap, design, sample, tools, analysis plan, ethics and timetable. Keep objectives measurable.

When interpreting, link each result to your question. A made-up survey of 200 civil servants had 150 usable replies. Response rate = 150 ÷ 200 = 75%. If 90 of the 150 said they had used an online service, that is 90 ÷ 150 = 60%. Report the base and the limitation: only 150 replied, so the result describes respondents, not all civil servants.

keyPoints: Research design must fit the question; quantitative, qualitative and mixed designs answer different kinds of question.
A literature review identifies themes and the gap, not just summaries of studies.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling does not.
Questionnaires and interviews need piloting and clear, non-leading questions.
Ethics require informed consent, voluntary participation, anonymity or confidentiality, data protection and approval.
A proposal should state measurable objectives and an analysis plan; interpret findings with response rates and limitations.

en.title: Advanced Theories of Public Administration
en.short: Institutionalism, public choice, principal-agent, network governance and critical theories compared for reform.

sections.heading: Institutions and choice
sections.text: Institutionalism holds that formal rules, informal norms and routines shape administrative behaviour. Historical institutionalism stresses path dependence: earlier choices constrain later reform. Sociological institutionalism explains that organisations adopt practices to gain legitimacy. Public choice applies economic reasoning to politics. It treats voters, politicians and officials as pursuing their own interests, so it predicts rent-seeking (gain through political influence rather than production) and budget maximisation. Institutionalism expects gradual change within inherited rules; public choice expects reforms that change incentives, such as competition or transparency.

sections.heading: Delegation and networks
sections.text: Principal-agent theory examines delegation. A principal, such as a minister, hires an agent, such as a chief executive. Information asymmetry, where the agent knows more than the principal, lets the agent shirk or pursue private goals. This creates agency costs, the costs of monitoring and the residual loss that remains even after monitoring. Tools include contracts, reporting and incentives. Network governance sees public problems as too complex for one organisation. State agencies, firms, civil society and citizens depend on one another, so coordination rests on trust, shared norms and informal authority. Reform then means building partnerships and steering networks, not only hierarchy.

sections.heading: Critical perspectives
sections.text: Critical perspectives ask whose interests administration serves. Marxist analysis links administrative power to capital and class. Feminist analysis examines gendered divisions of labour and exclusion. Postcolonial analysis questions imported models and local elite capture, where elites divert benefits to themselves. Interpretive approaches study how officials understand their work. These views challenge the claim that administration is neutral and warn that managerial reforms can narrow accountability to efficiency.

sections.heading: Case and comparison
sections.text: A made-up case: Amina leads a state water ministry. It contracts Kola’s agency to maintain rural pumps. Institutionalism explains why old procurement routines persist. Public choice predicts Kola may seek a larger budget. Principal-agent theory suggests performance contracts and audits. Network governance highlights village committees and spare-part suppliers. Critical theory asks whether women and poor households are heard. No theory is complete: use several to explain behaviour and design reform.

keyPoints: Institutionalism explains continuity through rules, norms and path dependence.
Public choice predicts self-interested behaviour, rent-seeking and budget growth.
Principal-agent theory addresses delegation, information asymmetry and agency costs.
Network governance explains coordination through trust and interdependence.
Critical perspectives question neutrality, power and exclusion.
Use several theories together to explain behaviour and reform.

en.title: Governance, Institutions and Public Value
en.short: Governance networks, institutional design, accountability, public value and state, market and civil society roles.

sections.heading: Governance as networks
sections.text: Governance is the process of steering collective action, not only the work of government. Public problems cross departmental and sector boundaries, so policies are delivered through networks: stable sets of state, market and civil society actors who exchange resources and information. Networks share knowledge and build trust, but they blur responsibility. A ministry, a private contractor and a community group may all shape a service. Analysis asks who is included, what each actor brings, and how conflict is settled.

sections.heading: Designing institutions
sections.text: Institutions are the rules, norms and organisations that structure behaviour. Institutional design means choosing those rules deliberately: who has authority, how decisions are made, how performance is rewarded, and how disputes are resolved. Good design fits the local context, creates credible commitment and avoids concentrating power. Elinor Ostrom’s work on common-pool resources (shared goods that users can overuse, such as fisheries or forests) showed that user-made rules can work with clear boundaries, graduated sanctions and accessible conflict resolution. Design distributes benefits and costs.

sections.heading: Accountability chains
sections.text: Accountability has two parts: answerability, the duty to explain decisions, and enforcement, the possibility of consequences. Vertical accountability runs through elections and citizens; horizontal accountability through courts, auditors and legislatures; social accountability through media and civil society. Networks make accountability harder because tasks are shared. Contracts, performance agreements, transparency and complaint channels help, but they do not replace public authority.

sections.heading: Public value roles
sections.text: Public value is what citizens collectively value and what public managers can legitimately create: outcomes, trust and fairness. Mark Moore’s strategic triangle asks whether a proposal is publicly valuable, politically and legally supported, and operationally feasible. The state sets rules and funds services; markets coordinate production and innovation; civil society voices needs and builds trust. In a made-up city case, the health ministry, a private clinic chain and a residents’ association run a maternal service. Clear roles, shared data and a complaints committee create value; unclear contracts shift blame.

keyPoints: Governance is steering through networks of state, market and civil society, not only government action.
Institutional design sets rules on authority, incentives and dispute resolution, and it distributes benefits and costs.
Accountability requires both answerability and consequences, through vertical, horizontal and social channels.
Public value is created when outcomes, trust and fairness are valued by citizens and legitimately produced.
Moore’s strategic triangle tests public value, political and legal support, and operational feasibility.
Clear roles and shared information in networks make accountability and value creation easier.

en.title: Advanced Public Financial Management and Fiscal Governance
en.short: Fiscal rules, medium-term frameworks, performance budgeting, debt dynamics and transparency.

sections.heading: Rules and frameworks
sections.text: Fiscal rules are numerical limits on budgets, such as a maximum deficit or debt ratio. They aim to build credibility, but can be procyclical and invite creative accounting. A medium-term expenditure framework (MTEF) sets sector ceilings for three or more years and links policy priorities to the annual budget. It is a rolling commitment, not a forecast. Countries differ: Nigeria’s Fiscal Responsibility Act 2007 created a Fiscal Responsibility Commission and requires MTEFs; South Africa’s Public Finance Management Act 1999 gives strong powers to the Treasury; Ghana’s Public Financial Management Act 2016 sets similar rules. Check current national law because rules change.

sections.heading: Performance and transparency
sections.text: Performance budgeting links funds to outputs or outcomes, often through programme budgets. It needs reliable cost and performance data, so it works better where accounting and audit are strong. Fiscal transparency means open, timely publication of budget documents, debt data and audit reports. The IMF Fiscal Transparency Code and the PEFA framework are widely used assessments. Institutions matter: the finance ministry, legislature, supreme audit institution, debt management office and independent fiscal councils. A fiscal council gives public analysis of forecasts and rule compliance. Transparency lets citizens and markets judge whether promises are kept.

sections.heading: Debt dynamics example
sections.text: Debt management balances cost against risk: maturity, currency and interest-rate exposure. Debt sustainability compares debt with GDP and with revenue. A simple debt ratio arithmetic: if debt rises 10% and nominal GDP rises 6%, a 50% debt-to-GDP ratio becomes 0.50 × 1.10 ÷ 1.06 = 0.519, or 51.9%. The ratio rises because debt grows faster than GDP. A primary surplus can offset this. Debt offices should publish a debt management strategy.

keyPoints: Fiscal rules are numerical limits on deficits, debt or spending, and their credibility depends on enforcement.
An MTEF is a rolling multi-year framework that sets sector ceilings and links policy to the annual budget.
Performance budgeting ties funding to outputs or outcomes but needs reliable cost and performance data.
Debt ratio next = current ratio × (1 + debt growth) ÷ (1 + nominal GDP growth).
Fiscal transparency requires timely, open budget, debt and audit information.
Country rules and institutions differ, so check the current national law and official documents.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Dissertation
en.short: Designs, case study, mixed methods, theory building, ethics, proposal writing and dissertation analysis.

sections.heading: Designs and questions
sections.text: A master’s dissertation answers a focused question with a design that fits it. Quantitative designs test hypotheses and estimate relationships. Advanced options include experiments, quasi-experiments, surveys and longitudinal panels, which follow the same people over time. Qualitative designs explore meaning and process. Common approaches are ethnography (observing a setting), grounded theory (building theory from data), phenomenology (studying lived experience) and case study. The question, not fashion, should drive the choice.

sections.heading: Case study and mixed methods
sections.text: A case study examines one bounded system, such as a local government or a reform programme, in depth. It can use documents, interviews and observation. Mixed methods combine qualitative and quantitative work. In a convergent design, both are collected in parallel and merged. In an explanatory sequential design, quantitative results are followed by qualitative work to explain them. In an exploratory sequential design, qualitative findings help build a survey or experiment. Theory building moves between concepts, propositions and evidence, and tests rival explanations.

sections.heading: Data, ethics, proposal
sections.text: Data quality depends on validity, reliability and trustworthiness. Triangulation (using several sources), member checking (checking findings with participants) and saturation (when new data add little) support qualitative work. Quantitative work needs good measurement, low missing data and checks for bias. Ethics require informed consent (voluntary agreement after information), confidentiality, no harm, and approval from a research ethics committee. Data protection law differs by country, so check the local rule. A proposal states the problem, literature gap, question, design, sampling, instruments, analysis plan, timeline, budget and ethics.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text: Qualitative analysis may use thematic coding (labelling repeated ideas) or framework analysis (a matrix of themes and cases). Quantitative analysis may use regression or other models, with robustness checks. Suppose Amina studies revenue collection in a made-up district. She interviews five officials, surveys 100 taxpayers and compares records. She reports response rates, coding decisions and limits. Academic writing presents a clear argument, cites sources honestly, avoids plagiarism and states limitations. The dissertation should show method, evidence and reasoning, not just length.

keyPoints: The research question should determine the design, not fashion.
Case study examines one bounded system in depth.
Mixed methods may be convergent, explanatory sequential or exploratory sequential.
Theory building links concepts, propositions and evidence and tests rival explanations.
Data quality rests on validity, reliability, trustworthiness and careful sampling.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm and ethics approval.
